{{Short description|Probability theorem}}
In [[probability theory]], '''Le Cam's theorem''', named after [[Lucien Le Cam]], states the following.<ref name=LeCam:1960 /><ref name=LeCam:1963 /><ref name=Steele:1994 />

Suppose:

* <math>X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots </math> are [[statistical independence|independent]] [[random variable]]s, each with a [[Bernoulli distribution]] (i.e., equal to either 0 or 1), not necessarily identically distributed.
* <math>\Pr(X_i = 1) = p_i, \text{ for } i = 1, 2, 3, \ldots.</math>
* <math>\lambda_n = p_1 + \cdots + p_n.</math>
* <math>S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n.</math>  (i.e. <math>S_n</math> follows a [[Poisson binomial distribution]])

Then

:<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty \left| \Pr(S_n=k) - {\lambda_n^k e^{-\lambda_n} \over k!} \right| < 2 \left( \sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2 \right). </math>

In other words, the sum has approximately a [[Poisson distribution]] and the above inequality bounds the approximation error in terms of the [[Total variation distance of probability measures|total variation distance]].

By setting ''p''<sub>''i''</sub> = ''λ''<sub>''n''</sub>/''n'', we see that this generalizes the usual [[Poisson limit theorem]].

When <math>\lambda_n</math> is large a better bound is possible: <math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty \left| \Pr(S_n=k) - {\lambda_n^k e^{-\lambda_n} \over k!} \right| < 2 \left(1 \wedge \frac 1 \lambda_n\right) \left( \sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2 \right)</math>,<ref name=denHollander:2012 /> where <math>\wedge</math> represents the <math>\min</math> operator. 

It is also possible to weaken the independence requirement.<ref name=denHollander:2012 />
